bodyLines.text: The process of intellectual property management
Quarterly research report is written up by the 27. ______
Deliver the report to 28. ______ to make amendments
In the review meeting, 29. ______ will check all the amendments
The final decision will be sent to the 30. ______ to analyze the cost of the whole process.

transcript.text: Now turn to Section 3.
Section 3.
You will hear two business students talking about the research they have done into one area of business.
First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26.
Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26.
Student A: Okay, so let's look at what topic we've got for the next tutorial.
Oh, intellectual property.
That's anything that you produce from your own ideas or creative activity.
It's like the property of your mind.
Student B: And we have to look at the different ways of legally protecting these ideas and inventions.
Student A: Right, we need to know what they are and be able to talk about them.
You want to start with copyright?
Student B: Yeah, it's the one I knew a bit about already.
It's your right as the author or inventor lasting for 70 years after your death.
It's free and you don't even have to apply for it.
Student A: But it doesn't fit every situation does it?
Okay, what about some other kinds of registration?
Hmm, I did some research on patents.
Student B: Right, a patent means no one else can financially benefit from your invention.
Student A: Right, it seems to be very costly to apply for.
So you really need to know what you've invented is worth going through all the rigmarole for.
Student B: Well, I don't think it's something you can do without professional help.
It's a very complicated process.
Student A: Let's have a look at trademarks next.
We are both quite familiar with these.
I mean, just think how well known the logos of some companies are.
They seem to really instill trust in a brand.
And so they add millions of dollars to how much a company's worth.
Student B: And from what I've discovered, it doesn't seem to cost much to register trademarks either.
Okay, so what's next? Ah, design.
This has quite a specific meaning as it relates to how something looks and not how it works.
I read it's standard for the big corporations that make mobile phones to register the design of their handsets,
so they remain quite distinctive.
Student A: That's interesting. I wasn't aware of that.
So how does design differ from the next category of protection?
Student B: You mean circuit?
Well, circuits are a type of protection that safeguards original layout design for things like computer chips.
So it's fairly narrow in its meaning.
And it is quite limited as it can only be enforced in this country.
Student A: Yeah, the blueprint could be copied and reproduced in other countries.
And the owner has no legal protection.
So my view is, what's the point?
Student B: Maybe in time it will be recognized elsewhere.
Student A: I find the next category quite interesting.
When I think of trade secrets, I immediately think of Granny May's cookies.
They've deliberately not patented their special recipes so that the other manufacturers don't know what the ingredients are.
Hard for them to discover.
Student B: Yeah, but it must be difficult to maintain a trade secret because you have to make sure that all staff sign an agreement and stick to it if they leave.
Student A: That's true.
Okay, so we're happy with what we've discussed with different types of intellectual property.
Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.
Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.
Student A: Next, we have to write up the process that one company uses to manage its intellectual property.
Student B: Yeah, in the company we looked at, there were certainly a lot of people involved in this process from the research leader through to the commercialization committee.
Student A: Right. Well, it all gets initiated by the quarterly research report.
This is produced by the, let me look at my notes.
The project leader.
They have to write up the report with details of how they are meeting their research deadlines.
Student B: And they put details in it about changes in intellectual property, don't they?
Things like they now realize that they are researching something that may be patentable after all.
And they have to identify this as early as possible.
Student A: And do they send the report to an external expert at this stage?
Student B: No, they send it on to the commercialization committee, which consists of the program leader and an industry representative.
They review the report, bearing amendments to the intellectual property.

Student A: Right. Then from that review meeting, all the amendments are brought together and gone through by the delivery officer who works out the most beneficial way to register the intellectual property.
Student B: Yes, this stage can take quite a long time. The project leader must get really frustrated by all this.
If I've got this right, they then let the business manager know what has been decided.
And it's at this point that the intellectual property gets taken out of the control of the research area,
and it becomes more to do with the financial or commercial issues of registration.
Student A: Exactly. So if they feel that their proposal fits within the allocated budget for intellectual property,
and a likely return on the investment is worth it, they will then need to engage the help of a specialist in the field.
It's extremely likely that they will find themselves.
That is the end of section three. You now have half a minute to check your answers.
